sp.speaker: Pythias
sp.l: First in this prayer I honor above all gods
the primal prophetess, Earth; and after her, Themis,
who second took her seat upon this
oracular throne of her mother, as a story tells; and in the third
allotment, by her consent and with no force from any,
another Titaness, child of Earth, took her seat here,
Phoebe; and she gave it as a birthday gift
to Phoebus, who bears his name derived from Phoebe.
Leaving the lake and rocky ridge of Delos,
he landed on the ship-frequented shores of Pallas
and came to this land and the dwellings of Parnassus.
They escorted him and held him in great reverence,
the road-building sons of Hephaestus, making
the untamed earth into a tamed land.
When he arrived, the people paid him great honor,
and Delphus, lord and helmsman of this country.
Zeus inspired his mind with the prophetic art
and established him fourth seer upon these thrones;
and Loxias is the spokesman of Zeus his father.
These gods I invoke in the prelude of my prayers.
Pallas of the Fore-Temple is also honored in my words;
and I revere the Nymphs where the Corycian rock
lies hollow, beloved of birds, the haunt of spirits.
Bromius holds the region—nor do I forget him—
ever since the god led the Bacchants in battle
and contrived for Pentheus a death like a hunted hare.
Calling upon the springs of Plistus, the might of Poseidon,
and Zeus the Most High, the Fulfiller,
I then take my seat as prophetess upon the throne.
May they grant me now to obtain far the best fortune
of all my former entrances; and if any Greeks are here,
let them enter as the lot assigns, according to custom;
for I prophesy as the god leads me.

sp.speaker: Pythias
sp.l: Things dreadful to tell, dreadful for eyes to behold,
have sent me back out of the house of Loxias,
so that I have neither strength nor power to lift my steps;
I run with my hands, not with swiftness of legs,
for a frightened old woman is nothing—no better than a child.
I was making my way toward the garlanded inner shrine,
and I see at the navel-stone a man hateful to the gods
occupying the suppliant's seat, his hands
dripping with blood, holding a newly drawn sword
and a high-grown branch of olive,
duly wreathed with a great tuft of wool,
a gleaming fleece; for on this point I will speak clearly.
In front of this man a wondrous band
of women sleeps, seated upon thrones.
No, not women, but Gorgons I call them—
nor yet can I liken them to Gorgon shapes.
Once before I saw painted creatures carrying off
the banquet of Phineus; yet these are wingless to behold,
black, and utterly loathsome in every way.
They snore with blasts no one can approach,
and from their eyes they drip a hateful ooze;
and their attire is fit to bring neither before the images
of the gods nor into the roofs of men.
The tribe of this company I have never seen,
nor what land boasts of breeding this race
with impunity without groaning afterward for its labor.
From here on, let what follows be the care
of the master of this house himself, mighty Loxias;
for he is a healer-prophet and reader of portents,
and for others too a purifier of households.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: I will not betray you; to the very end your guardian,
standing close beside you and even when far away,
I will not be gentle to your enemies.
Even now you see these raging creatures caught;
fallen in sleep are the loathsome maidens,
aged ancient children, with whom mingles
no god, nor man, nor any beast ever.
For the sake of evils they were born, since they inhabit
evil darkness and Tartarus beneath the earth,
objects of hatred to men and to the Olympian gods.
Nevertheless, flee and do not grow faint;
for they will drive you even across the long mainland
as you stride ever over the wanderer-trodden earth,
and over the sea and sea-girt cities.
Do not grow weary beforehand, brooding on this
toil; go to the city of Pallas
and sit clasping her ancient image in your arms.
There, with judges of this cause and soothing
words, we shall find means
to release you completely from these toils;
for it was I who persuaded you to slay your mother's body.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: Lord Apollo, you know how not to do wrong;
and since you know this, learn also not to neglect me.
Your power to do good is a sure pledge.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Remember, let not fear overcome your mind.
And you, my own brother in blood and of a common father,
Hermes, guard him; true to your title,
be his Escort, shepherding this
my suppliant—Zeus indeed respects this right of outlaws—
as he sets forth with fair-escorting fortune among mortals.

sp.speaker: Klytaimestras Eidolon
sp.l: You would sleep, ah! And what use is there for sleepers?
While I, thus dishonored by you
among the other dead—for the reproach of those I slew
never ceases among the departed,
and I wander in disgrace; and I declare to you that
I bear the heaviest accusation from them;
yet though I suffered such dreadful things from my dearest kin,
not one of the spirits is wroth on my behalf,
slaughtered as I was by matricidal hands.
Behold these wounds in my heart, and whence they came!
For the sleeping mind is made bright with eyes,
whereas in daytime the fate of mortals is unforeseen.
Many indeed are the offerings of mine you have lapped up—
wineless libations, sobering appeasements,
and solemn nightly banquets upon the hearth of fire
I sacrificed, at an hour shared by no other of the gods.
And all these things I see trampled underfoot.
He has escaped and is gone like a fawn,
and lightly too out of the midst of the hunting-nets
he has bounded away, mocking you aloud.
Hear me, for I have spoken for my very
life: come to your senses, O goddesses beneath the earth!
For in a dream I, Clytemnestra, now call upon you.

sp.speaker: Klytaimestras Eidolon
sp.l: Whimper if you will, but the man is gone, fleeing far away;
for he has friends unlike mine.

sp.speaker: Klytaimestras Eidolon
sp.l: You slumber too deeply and do not pity my suffering;
Orestes, murderer of this mother, is gone.

sp.speaker: Klytaimestras Eidolon
sp.l: You groan, you slumber! Will you not rise at once?
What task is fated for you except to work harm?

sp.speaker: Klytaimestras Eidolon
sp.l: Sleep and toil, mighty conspirators,
have drained the fierceness of the dreadful she-dragon.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Seize him, seize him, seize him, seize him! Mark him well!

sp.speaker: Klytaimestras Eidolon
sp.l: In a dream you pursue your prey, and bay like
a hound that never gives up its care for the chase.
What are you doing? Rise up, let not weariness conquer you,
nor remain unaware of your loss, softened by sleep.
Feel the sting in your heart from just reproaches;
for to the wise they serve as goads.
Breathe your bloody blast upon him,
wither him with vapor, with the fire of your belly,
follow, waste him away with a renewed pursuit!

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Wake, wake her too, as I wake you!
Are you sleeping? Arise, and kicking off sleep,
let us see whether anything in this prelude is in vain.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Ah, ah, shame! We have suffered, sisters—
truly much have I suffered, and in vain—
we have suffered a bitter grief, alas,
an unbearable wrong!
Out of the nets the beast has fallen and is gone!
Overcome by sleep, I have lost my prey.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Oh, son of Zeus, you are a thief!
Young, you have ridden down aged goddesses,
honoring your suppliant, a godless man and
bitter to his parents;
the matricide you have stolen away, though you are a god!
Who will say that any of this is just?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Reproach coming to me from dreams
has struck me like a charioteer
with a goad grasped in the middle,
beneath my midriff, beneath my heart.
I feel the harsh, the crushing chill
of the public scourger's cruel lash.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Such are the deeds of the younger gods,
who rule all things beyond the bounds of justice—
a blood-dripping throne
about its foot, about its head!
One may behold earth's navel-stone taking upon itself
a dread pollution of blood to bear.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Though a prophet, with hearth-pollution
he has defiled his own shrine, self-impelled, self-invited,
honoring mortal things against the law of the gods,
and destroying the ancient apportionments.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Grievous to me too he is, yet him he shall not set free;
even fleeing beneath the earth he is never liberated.
Blood-guilty as he is, another avenger upon his head
from his own kin shall he acquire.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Out, I command you, from this house at once!
Go, begone from my prophetic shrine,
lest you receive a winged glistening serpent
sped from my golden bowstring
and in agony disgorge black foam drawn from men,
vomiting the clots of murder you have sucked.
It is not fitting for you to come near this house;
rather where beheadings and eye-gougings
are the sentences, and slaughters, and by destruction of seed
the vigor of boys is ruined, and mutilation,
and stoning, and men moan with long lamentation
impaled beneath the spine. Do you hear
what sort of feast you have a fondness for, loathed
by the gods? Every feature of your form reveals it.
The den of a blood-drinking lion
is the fitting home for such as you, not to rub your
pollution upon this nearby oracular shrine.
Go, roaming without a herdsman;
for to such a herd no god bears goodwill.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Lord Apollo, hear our side in turn.
You yourself are not merely an accomplice in this,
but you alone did the whole deed, bearing full guilt.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: How so? Extend your speech that far.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: You gave an oracle that the stranger should slay his mother.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: I gave an oracle to exact vengeance for his father. What then?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: And then you undertook to receive the fresh blood.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Yes, and I bade him turn as suppliant to this house.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: And do you then revile us who escorted him here?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Yes, for it is not fitting for you to come to this house.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Yet this office has been assigned to us.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: What honor is this? Boast of your fine privilege!

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: We drive matricides out from their homes.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: What then of a woman who slays her husband?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: That would not be kindred murder of one's own blood.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Truly you have made of no honor and set at naught
the pledges of Hera the Fulfiller and of Zeus!
Cypris too is cast aside in dishonor by this argument,
from whom come to mortals their dearest joys.
For the bed of man and wife, ordained by fate,
is greater than an oath, guarded by Justice.
If, then, toward those who slay one another you are lax,
neither exacting vengeance nor looking upon them in wrath,
I say you do not justly hound Orestes into exile.
For the one deed I see you taking deeply to heart,
while toward the other you clearly act more calmly.
The goddess Pallas shall oversee the trial of this cause.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: That man I will never, ever leave.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Pursue him, then, and give yourself more toil!

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Do not cut short my honors by your words.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: I would not even accept your honors to hold them.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Because in any case you are called great beside the throne of Zeus.
As for me—since a mother's blood drives me on—I shall
pursue this man for justice and hunt him down.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: And I will aid and rescue my suppliant;
for dreadful among mortals and among gods is
the wrath of a suppliant, if I willingly betray him.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: Queen Athena, at the commands of Loxias
I have come; receive kindly an outcast,
not one seeking purification nor with uncleansed hand,
but already blunted and worn away against
other houses and the beaten paths of mortals.
Crossing land and sea alike,
keeping the oracular injunctions of Loxias,
I approach your house and your image, goddess.
Keeping my post here, I await the issue of my trial.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Aha! Here is a clear trace of the man.
Follow the directions of our voiceless informer;
for like a hound tracking a wounded fawn,
by blood and drippings we hunt him out.
With many man-wearying toils my chest
pants; for every region of earth has been ranged over,
and over the sea in wingless flight
I came in pursuit, no slower than a ship.
And now here he is somewhere crouching down:
the scent of human blood smiles upon me.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Look, look sharply again!
Gaze everywhere, lest
escaping in flight unseen go
the matricide, unpunished!
Here again indeed, finding protection,
clasped around the image of the immortal goddess,
he wishes to stand trial for his deed.
That may not be! A mother's blood upon the ground
is hard to recover, alas!
The liquid spilled on earth is gone.
Rather, in return you must let me suck from your living limbs
the red clot; from you may I
draw the pasture of a bitter draught;
and having withered you alive, I will drag you down below,
to pay in recompense the penalty of matricidal woe.
And you shall see if any other mortal has sinned,
against god or guest
impiously or against dear parents,
each receiving the just deserts of justice.
For mighty Hades is the auditor of mortals
beneath the earth,
and surveys all things with his recording mind.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: Taught in misfortunes, I know
many rites of purification, and when it is right to speak
and likewise to keep silent; and in this present matter
I was commanded to speak by a wise teacher.
For the blood sleeps and fades from my hand,
and the matricidal pollution is washed away;
while still fresh, at the hearth of the god
Phoebus it was driven out by purifying sacrifices of swine.
It would be a long tale for me from the beginning,
how many I have approached in harmless converse.

l.del: Time, as it grows old, purifies all things alike.

sp.l: And now from pure lips I piously invoke
Athena, queen of this land, to come
to my aid; without the spear she shall win
both myself and my land and the Argive people
as a faithful and just ally for all time.
Whether in regions of the Libyan land,
around the stream of her native river Triton,
she plants her foot upright or covered by her robe,
aiding her friends, or surveys the Phlegraean plain
like a bold commander,
may she come—for a god hears even from afar—
that she may become my deliverer from these troubles.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Neither Apollo nor Athena's might
could rescue you from perishing
abandoned, not knowing where joy lies in your heart,
bloodless fodder for spirits, a shadow.
Do you not even answer, but spurn my words,
you who are fattened and consecrated to me?
Living you shall feast me, not even slain at an altar;
and you shall hear this hymn to bind you fast.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Come now, let us also join the dance, since
we have resolved to display
our hateful music,
and to declare how our company
dispenses the lots among mankind.
We claim to be upright in justice:
upon him who holds out clean hands
no wrath creeps from us,
and unharmed he passes through life;
but whoever has sinned like this man
and hides his blood-stained hands,
as upright witnesses for the dead
we appear beside him, exactors of blood,
revealed in full to him.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Mother who bore me, O Mother
Night, to the blind and to the seeing
a punishment, hear me! For Leto's
son robs me of honor,
snatching away this
cowering hare, my rightful
purification for a mother's murder.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Over the consecrated victim
this is our song: frenzy,
distraction, mind-destroying,
a hymn from the Erinyes,
binding the mind, without
lyre, a withering to mortals.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: For this lot all-piercing
Fate spun for us to hold steadfastly:
whenever upon mortals reckless
kin-murders fall,
to attend upon them until
he goes beneath the earth; and dead,
he is none too free.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Over the consecrated victim
this is our song: frenzy,
distraction, mind-destroying,
a hymn from the Erinyes,
binding the mind, without
lyre, a withering to mortals.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: At our birth these lots were ratified for us:
to keep our hands from the immortals, nor is any
a sharer of our feasts;
of pure-white robes I am allotted no portion or share.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: For I have chosen the overthrow
of houses, whenever Ares,
tame within the home, slays a kinsman.
Rushing thus upon him,
strong though he be, we dim
him because of the fresh blood.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: We are eager to relieve others of these cares
and by my offices to secure exemption for the gods,
that they need not come to trial;
for Zeus has deemed this blood-dripping, hateful tribe
unworthy of his converse.

l.add: For I have chosen the overthrow
tame within the home, slays a kinsman.
strong though he be, we dim
him because of the fresh blood.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: The glories of men, though very proud beneath the sky,
melt away beneath the earth and dwindle in dishonor
at our black-robed assaults and the
spiteful dances of our feet.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: For leaping high,
from above I bring down
the heavy-falling force of my foot,
limbs that trip even swift runners—
an unbearable ruin.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Falling, he does not know it through his mindless folly;
such for a dark cloud of pollution hovers over the man,
and a murky mist over his house is told
by a groan-filled rumor.

l.add: the heavy-falling force of my foot,
limbs that trip even swift runners—

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: For it abides: resourceful
and decisive, mindful of evil
deeds, dread
and hard for mortals to appease,
pursuing our unhonored, unprized
lots apart from the gods in sunless
gloom, a rugged, trackless path
for the seeing and the blind alike.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: What mortal, then, does not revere
and fear these things,
hearing from me the ordinance
ratified by Fate and granted
in full by the gods? Still to me
remains my ancient privilege, nor do I meet
with dishonor, even though beneath the earth
I hold my station and sunless darkness.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: From afar I heard the cry of a summons
from the Scamander, as I was taking possession of the land
which the leaders and chiefs of the Achaeans,
a great portion of their spear-won spoils,
assigned root and branch to me for all time,
a choice gift for the sons of Theseus.
From there I came speeding my unwearied foot,
without wings, rustling the fold of my aegis.

l.del: having yoked this chariot with vigorous steeds

sp.l: Seeing this strange company in my land,
I feel no fear, yet wonder is before my eyes.
Who are you? I speak to all in common:
both to this stranger seated at my image
and to you, who are like no race of begotten beings,
neither seen by the gods among goddesses
nor resembling mortal shapes.
Yet to speak ill of one's neighbors without cause
is far from justice, and right stands aloof from it.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: You shall learn everything briefly, daughter of Zeus.
We are the eternal children of Night;
Curses we are called in our homes beneath the earth.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: I know your race and the titles by which you are called.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: You shall quickly learn my honors as well.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: I would learn them, if someone speaks a plain account.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: We drive homicides out from their homes.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: And for the slayer, where is the goal of his flight?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Where joy is nowhere known.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Is it such a flight you are shrilling upon this man?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Yes, for he saw fit to be the murderer of his mother.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Under other compulsion, or fearing someone's wrath?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Where is there a goad so great as to compel matricide?

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Two parties are present, and only half the tale is here.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Yet he would neither accept an oath nor consent to give one.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: You wish to be called just rather than to act justly.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: How so? Instruct me, for you are not poor in wisdom.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: I say that unjust causes must not triumph through oaths.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Then examine the case, and judge a straight judgment.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Would you indeed entrust to me the decision of the charge?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Why not? We revere you as worthy and of worthy stock.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: What do you wish to say in turn to this, stranger?
Declare your country, your lineage, and your
misfortunes, and then ward off this charge—
if indeed, trusting in justice, you sit guarding
this image near my hearth,
a solemn suppliant after the manner of Ixion.
To all these questions give me a clear reply.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: Queen Athena, first from your last
words I will remove a great concern.
I am not a suppliant needing purification, nor with pollution
upon my hand did I sit at your image.
I will give you strong proof of this:
it is the law that a murderer remain voiceless
until at the hand of a purifier of blood
the slaughter of a young suckling beast stains him with blood.
Long ago at other houses we have been thus purified,
both with victims and with flowing streams.
This concern, then, I put out of the way.
My lineage you shall quickly learn.
I am an Argive, and my father you do well to ask of—
Agamemnon, marshal of seafaring men,
with whom you made Troy, the city of Ilium,
no city at all. He perished in no noble way upon returning
home; for my dark-hearted
mother slew him, shrouding him in cunning toils
that bore witness to his murder in the bath.
And I, returning home after my former exile,
slew her who bore me—I will not deny it—
in blood-for-blood vengeance for my dearest father.
For this deed Loxias shares responsibility,
proclaiming agonies to goad my heart
if I should fail to do this to the guilty.
Judge whether I acted justly or not;
however I fare in your hands, I shall accept it.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: The matter is too great for any mortal to think
he can judge it; nor yet is it lawful for me
to decide trials of murder that arouse fierce wrath—
especially since you have come to my house
a seasoned, pure, and harmless suppliant,
and thus being blameless I respect your right in my city;
while these have an office not easy to dismiss,
and if they do not win a victorious verdict,
hereafter venom from their spirits,
falling on the ground, will be an unbearable, lasting plague to the land.
So stands the case: either way, for them to stay
or to be sent away is fraught with hopeless harm for me.
Yet since this matter has alighted here,
I will choose sworn judges of homicide
and establish an ordinance for all time.
Summon your witnesses and proofs,
sworn testimonies to aid the cause of justice;
and having chosen the best of my citizens,
I will return to decide this case truly,
bound by oath to pronounce nothing unjust.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Now comes the overthrow of new
ordinances, if the cause
and wrong of this
matricide shall prevail.
At once this deed will reconcile all
mortals to recklessness;
and many real wounds inflicted by children
await parents
in time to come.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: For no wrath from us, the mortal-watching
Maenads, shall creep
upon their deeds—
I will let loose every form of death.
One shall ask of another, proclaiming
his neighbor's woes,
for a ceasing and abatement of troubles;
and uncertain remedies the wretch
indeed someone recommends in vain.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Let no one call out
when struck by calamity,
crying this word:
"O Justice,
O thrones of the Erinyes!"
Thus perhaps some father
or newly stricken mother
may wail their lament, now that
the house of Justice falls.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: There is a place where dread is good
and as overseer of the mind
must remain seated.
It is profitable
to learn wisdom under sorrow.
Who, if he does not nurture
his heart would in fear—
city or mortal alike—
would still revere Justice?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Neither an ungoverned life
nor one ruled by a despot
should you praise.
To every mean has God
granted power, though in different
ways he oversees different things.
I speak a word in due measure:
truly insolence is the child
of impiety;
while from health
of mind comes the all-beloved
and much-prayed-for prosperity.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: In sum I say to you:
revere the altar of Justice,
and do not,
with an eye to gain, with godless
foot kick it in dishonor;
for punishment will follow,
and the appointed end abides.
Therefore let each duly honor
reverence for parents
and respect the guest-honoring
visitations
of his house.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: He who is just willingly, without compulsion,
shall not be unblessed;
utterly destroyed indeed he can never be.
But the bold transgressor, I say,
who brings in a confused mass of cargo without justice,
in time by force shall strike
his sail, when trouble seizes him
and his yardarm shatters.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: He calls on those who do not hear in the midst
of the fierce-wrestling whirlpool;
and the spirit laughs at the reckless man,
seeing him who boasted it would never happen
helpless in inescapable woes, unable to round the headland;
having dashed his lifelong former wealth
against the reef of Justice,
he perishes unwept, unseen.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Herald, make proclamation and hold back the crowd;
and let the piercing Tyrrhenian
trumpet, filled with mortal breath,
sound forth its high-pitched call to the assembly.
For as this council-chamber fills,
it is fitting to keep silence and learn my ordinances—
both the whole city for all time to come
and these litigants, so that justice may be well decided.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Lord Apollo, rule over what is yours;
tell us what share you have in this matter.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: I have come both to bear witness—for by law
this man is a suppliant and hearth-guest of my
house, and I am the purifier of this bloodshed—
and myself to plead his cause; for I share the blame
for the slaying of his mother. Open the trial,
and as well as you know how, confirm this judgment.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: The word is yours, and I open the trial;
for the prosecutor, speaking first from the beginning,
would rightly instruct us in the case.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: We are many, yet we will speak concisely.
Answer word for word, taking your turn:
first tell us whether you killed your mother.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: I killed her; of that there is no denial.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: That is already one of the three wrestling falls.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: You make that boast over one who is not yet down.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Yet you must say how you killed her.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: I say it: with sword-drawn hand, cutting her throat.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: By whom were you persuaded, and by whose counsels?

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: By this god's oracles; and he bears witness for me.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: The prophet instructed you to commit matricide?

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: Yes, and up to now I do not blame my fortune.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Wait until the vote catches you—you will soon speak otherwise.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: I am confident; my father will send aid from the grave.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Trust in the dead now, after killing your mother!

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: For she was stained with the taint of two pollutions.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: How so? Explain this to the judges.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: In murdering her husband, she slew my father.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Yet you live, while she is free by her death.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: Why did you not drive her into exile while she lived?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: She was not of one blood with the man she slew.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: And am I of one blood with my mother?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: How else could she have nourished you within her, murderer,
beneath her girdle? Do you disown a mother's dearest blood?

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: Now bear witness, and expound for me,
Apollo, whether I slew her with justice.
For having done the deed as it stands I do not deny;
but whether this bloodshed seems just or not to your mind,
judge, so that I may declare it to these judges.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: I will speak justly before you, this great tribunal
of Athena—and being a prophet I will not lie.
Never yet have I spoken upon my prophetic throne,
concerning man, woman, or city,
anything that Zeus, father of the Olympians, did not command.
Learn how strong this plea of justice is,
and I bid you follow the will of my father;
for an oath is in no way stronger than Zeus.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Zeus, as you say, gave this oracle,
to tell Orestes here, in avenging his father's murder,
to pay no regard at all to a mother's honor?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Yes, for it is not the same thing for a noble man to die,
honored with a scepter given by Zeus,
and that at a woman's hand—not by fierce
far-shooting arrows, as from an Amazon,
but as you shall hear, Pallas, and you who sit
to decide this matter by your vote.
Returning from the campaign, having fared

l.sic: for the most part well, she welcomed him with kindly words;
as he stepped from the bath, at the end

sp.l: she cast a cloak over him like a tent, and in an endless
embroidered robe she tangled and struck down her husband.
Such, as I have told you, was the death of the man,
all-revered, the commander of the fleet.
Her I have described as such, that the people may be stung to anger,
who have been appointed to decide this trial.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Zeus honors a father's death more, by your account;
yet he himself bound his aged father Cronus.
How does what you say not contradict that?
I call you to witness that you hear these words!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: O all-hated monsters, loathed by the gods,
fetters he could unloose—there is a remedy for that
and many a means of release;
but once the dust has drunk up a man's blood
when he is dead, there is no rising up again.
For that my father has made no incantations,
though all other things he turns upside down and
orders without panting at all in his strength.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: See how you plead for this man's acquittal:
having poured out his mother's kindred blood upon the ground,
shall he then dwell in his father's house in Argos?
What public altars shall he use?
What lustral water of the brotherhoods will admit him?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: This too I will explain, and learn how rightly I speak.
She who is called the mother of the child is not
its parent, only the nurse of the newly sown seed;
he who mounts begets, while she, like a stranger for a stranger,
preserves the young shoot, for those whom a god does not blight.
I will show you a proof of this argument:
a father can beget without a mother; close by
stands a witness, the child of Olympian Zeus,
not nurtured in the darkness of a womb,
yet such a shoot as no goddess could bear.
And I, Pallas, both in all other ways as I know how,
will make your city and your people great,
and I sent this man as hearth-guest to your house
so that he might be faithful for all time,
and that you, goddess, might win him as an ally,
and those after him, and that it might abide forever
for their descendants to cherish these pledges.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Shall I now bid these judges cast a just vote
according to their conscience, since enough has been said?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: For our part, every arrow has already been shot;
I wait to hear how the contest will be decided.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Well then, how shall I order this so as to be blameless in your eyes?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: You have heard what you have heard; as you cast your vote,
revere your oath in your hearts, strangers.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Hear now my ordinance, people of Attica,
judging the first trial for bloodshed.
Henceforth for the people of Aegeus this council
of judges shall exist forever.
And this Hill of Ares, the seat and tents of the Amazons
when they came campaigning out of grudge against Theseus,
and built this new-founded
high-towered citadel against his towers,
and sacrificed to Ares—whence the rock takes its name,
the Hill of Ares: upon this hill, Reverence
of the citizens and her kinsman Fear shall restrain
wrongdoing by day and by night alike,
so long as the citizens themselves do not pollute the laws
with evil innovations; for if you foul bright water
with mud, you will never find a drink.
Neither anarchy nor despotism
do I counsel my citizens to uphold and revere,
nor to cast all dread out of the city;
for what mortal is just who fears nothing?
Rightly standing in awe of such majesty,
you will possess a bulwark of the land and salvation of the city
such as no other mortals possess,
neither among the Scythians nor in the realms of Pelops.
Untouched by gain, this council—
reverend, quick to wrath, a wakeful
sentinel of the land on behalf of those who sleep—I establish.
This exhortation I have spoken at length to my
citizens for the future; now you must rise,
take up your ballots, and decide the trial,
revering your oath. My word is spoken.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Indeed, this grievous company in your land
I advise you by no means to dishonor.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: And I bid you fear the oracles, both mine and those of Zeus,
and not render them fruitless.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Yet you concern yourself with bloody deeds not allotted to you,
and no longer pure will be the oracles you dispense.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Did my father then err in his counsels
at the first supplication for bloodshed, that of Ixion?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Talk on; but if I do not win this case,
I will haunt this land again as a heavy burden.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Yet both among the younger and the older
gods you are without honor; and I shall win.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Such things you did in the house of Pheres too:
you persuaded the Fates to make mortals immortal.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Is it not just to benefit one who reveres you,
especially whenever he happens to be in need?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: It was you who destroyed the ancient apportionments
and beguiled the ancient goddesses with wine.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Soon you, failing to win the verdict of this trial,
will vomit your venom—no burden at all to your foes.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Since you, a young god, ride down my age,
I wait to hear the outcome of this trial,
still undecided whether to vent my wrath upon the city.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: It is my task to cast the final judgment;
and this ballot I shall add to Orestes' side.
For there is no mother who gave me birth,
and I commend the male in all things, save entering marriage,
with all my heart, and am wholly on the father's side.
Thus I will not set higher value on the death of a woman
who slew her husband, the guardian of the house.
Orestes wins, even if the votes are judged equal.
Turn out the ballots from the urns as quickly as possible,
you judges to whom this office has been assigned.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: O Phoebus Apollo, how will the contest be decided?

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: O dark Mother Night, do you behold these things?

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: Now comes the noose's end for me, or to look upon the light.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: And for us, to perish or to wield our honors henceforth.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.l: Count rightly the ballots cast out, strangers,
revering justice in the division.
When judgment is lacking, great harm ensues,
and a single cast ballot has set upright a house.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: This man has escaped the charge of bloodshed;
for the count of the ballots is equal.

sp.speaker: Orestes
sp.l: O Pallas, O savior of my house!
Deprived of my fatherland, it is you who
have restored me to my home; and a Greek shall say:

l.q: The man of Argos once more dwells in his father's
estate, through the grace of Pallas and Loxias,
and of the third, the all-accomplishing

sp.l: Savior, who, respecting my father's death,
saves me, looking upon these advocates of my mother.
And I, to this land and to your people,
for all the fullness of time hereafter,
having sworn an oath, now depart to my home:
that no helmsman of my land shall ever
come hither bringing a well-equipped spear.
For we ourselves, though then in our graves,
upon those who transgress my present oaths
will inflict hopeless disasters,
making their marches dispirited and their crossings ill-omened,
so that they repent their undertaking;
but if they keep it upright, and ever honor
this city of Pallas with allied spear,
to them we shall be all the more gracious.
Farewell, both you and your city-guarding people:
may you hold an inescapable grip over your foes,
bringing safety and victory in war.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Ah, you younger gods, you have ridden down
the ancient laws and wrenched them from my hands!
And I, dishonored, wretched, heavy with wrath,
in this land, alas,
venom, venom in requital for my grief
will let drop from my heart, a dripping
unbearable to the earth; and from it
a blight, leafless, childless—
O Justice!—rushing over the plain
shall cast man-destroying stains upon the land.
I groan: what shall I do?
I am mocked by the citizens!
Unbearable is what I have suffered!
Ah, deeply ill-fated are the daughters
of Night, grieving in dishonor!

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Be persuaded by me not to bear this with heavy groans;
for you have not been defeated, but an equal-voted verdict
truly came forth, with no dishonor to you.
Rather, clear testimony from Zeus was present,
and he himself who gave the oracle was himself the witness
that Orestes should suffer no harm for doing this.
Do not be angry, nor bring down heavy wrath
upon this land, nor cause barrenness
by letting fall droppings of spirits,
fierce spears that devour the seeds.
For I promise you in all justice
seats and caverns in a righteous land,
where seated upon shining thrones at hearths
you shall be held in honor by these citizens.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Ah, you younger gods, you have ridden down
the ancient laws and wrenched them from my hands!
And I, dishonored, wretched, heavy with wrath,
in this land, alas,
venom, venom in requital for my grief
will let drop from my heart, a dripping
unbearable to the earth; and from it
a blight, leafless, childless—
O Justice!—rushing over the plain
shall cast man-destroying stains upon the land.
I groan: what shall I do?
I am mocked by the citizens!
Unbearable is what I have suffered!
Ah, deeply ill-fated are the daughters
of Night, grieving in dishonor!

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: You are not dishonored; do not in excessive rage,
goddesses, make the land of mortals past healing.
I too trust in Zeus—what need to say it?—
and I alone of the gods know the keys of the chamber
in which the thunderbolt is sealed.
Yet there is no need of it; be persuaded by me
and cast not from a reckless tongue words upon the earth
causing all things that bear fruit to fare ill.
Lull to sleep the bitter fury of the black wave,
as an august sharer of my honors and my home;
receiving forever from this broad land firstfruits
as offerings for children and the rite of marriage,
you will praise these words of mine.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: That I should suffer this, alas!
That I, of ancient wisdom, should dwell beneath the earth,
alas, an unhonored pollution!
I breathe out fury and all my wrath!
Oh, oh, Earth, alas!
What anguish steals into my sides, what pain?
Hear my passion, Mother
Night! For from my ancient
honors, the gods' hard-to-wrestle
wiles have swept me away as naught.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: I will bear with your anger, for you are older;
and in that indeed you are far wiser than I,
yet Zeus has granted no mean understanding to me as well.
If you go to a foreign land,
you will come to long for this country—I foretell it.
For oncoming time shall bring greater honor
to these citizens; and you, holding an honored
seat beside the house of Erechtheus,
shall receive from processions of men and women
such honors as you could never obtain from any other mortals.
Do not cast upon my territory
bloody whetstones, ruinous to the hearts
of the young, maddened with wineless rage,
nor, plucking out as it were the heart of fighting cocks,
implant among my citizens civil war
and bold fury against one another.
Let war be abroad, readily at hand,
in which there shall be a fierce love of glory;
the battle of the household bird I will not have.
Such terms are yours to choose from me:
doing good, receiving good, well honored,
to share in this land most beloved of the gods.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: That I should suffer this, alas!
That I, of ancient wisdom, should dwell beneath the earth,
alas, an unhonored pollution!
I breathe out fury and all my wrath!
Oh, oh, Earth, alas!
What anguish steals into my sides, what pain?
Hear my passion, Mother
Night! For from my ancient
honors, the gods' hard-to-wrestle
wiles have swept me away as naught.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: I will not tire of telling you of these blessings,
so that you may never say that by me, a younger goddess,
and by my city-guarding mortals, you, an ancient goddess,
were driven away dishonored, banished from this soil.
If you hold in awe the sacred majesty of Persuasion,
the soothing charm and enchantment of my tongue,
then stay; but if you do not wish to stay,
you could not justly bring down upon this city
any wrath or anger or harm upon its people.
For it is in your power to be a sharer of this land
with all justice and honored forever.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Queen Athena, what seat do you say I shall hold?

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: One free from all woe; accept it.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Suppose I have accepted: what honor awaits me?

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: That no house shall prosper without you.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Will you bring this about, so that I have such power?

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Yes, for we will prosper the fortunes of him who reveres you.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: And will you give me a pledge for all time?

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Yes, for I need not promise what I will not fulfill.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: You seem to charm me, and I lay aside my wrath.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Therefore, dwelling in this land, you shall win friends.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: What blessings, then, do you bid me chant over this land?

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Such as aim at no evil victory,
coming both from the earth, from the sea's dew,
and from heaven; and that the blasts of the winds
blowing with fair sunlight may pass over the land;
that the fruit of the earth and abundant increase of flocks,
flourishing for the citizens, may never fail with time,
and that mortal seed be kept safe.
May you be more favorable to the pious;
for I love, like a gardener tending his plants,
the race of these righteous men, untouched by grief.
Such is your part; and in the famed contests of war,
I will not fail to honor
this city victorious among mortals.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: I will accept a home with Pallas,
nor will I dishonor the city
which almighty Zeus and Ares
hold as the stronghold of the gods,
the altar-guarding jewel of the gods of Greece.
For her I pray,
prophesying graciously,
that abundant blessings of life
may be made to spring from the earth
by the bright radiance of the sun.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: This I gladly accomplish for these
citizens, settling here these great
and hard-to-appease deities.
For to them it has been allotted
to order all human affairs.
He who has not met them in their wrath
knows not whence come the blows of life;
for the sins of his forebears
hale him before them, and silent destruction
levels even the loud boaster
in hostile anger.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Let no tree-blighting harm blow—
I speak my favor—
and let no scorching heat that blinds the buds
cross the borders of this land;
let no barren, lingering plague creep near;
may the earth nourish flourishing flocks
with twin offspring
at the appointed season; and ever may the wealth-bringing
offspring of the earth honor
the lucky gift of the gods.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Do you hear, bulwark of the city,
what she ordains? For great is the power
of the dread Erinys both among the immortals
and those beneath the earth, and regarding mankind
they manifestly bring all to fulfillment,
granting to some songs, and to others
a life dimmed with tears.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Untimely, man-destroying
chances I forbid;
and to lovely maidens
grant lives blessed with husbands,
you who hold authority,
and you goddesses, O Fates,
sisters by one mother,
spirits who dispense rightly,
sharers of every house,
weighty at every season
with righteous visitations,
most honored everywhere among the gods.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: That these blessings are graciously
ordained for my land
I rejoice; and I love the eyes of Persuasion,
because she watched over my tongue and lips
when they fiercely refused me.
Zeus of the Assembly has prevailed,
and our rivalry in good
triumphs forever.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: And civil strife, insatiable of evils,
I pray may never roar
within this city.
Nor may the dust, drinking
the black blood of citizens,
through passion for vengeance
seize upon retaliatory
slaughters in the city.
Rather may they return joy for joy
with a mind of common love,
and hate with one accord;
for this is the cure of many ills among mortals.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Are they not wise to find
the path of fair speech?
From these fearful countenances
I see great gain for these citizens;
for if, ever kindly to these Kindly Ones,
you greatly honor them, you shall shine forth
guiding both land and city
in straight justice everywhere.

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Rejoice, rejoice in your due portions of wealth!
Rejoice, people of the city,
seated close to Zeus,
dear to the dear maiden goddess,
learning wisdom in due time.
Beneath the wings of Pallas,
the Father holds you in reverence.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: Rejoice, you too! Now I must go
first to show you your chambers
by the sacred light of these escorts.
Go, and sped beneath these solemn sacrifices
into the earth, hold back what is ruinous
to the land, and send forth what is profitable
for the city's victory.
And do you lead the way, city-guarding
children of Cranaus, for these new dwellers.
May the citizens hold
good intent for good deeds!

sp.speaker: Choros
sp.l: Rejoice, rejoice again—I double the cry—
all you throughout the city,
both spirits and mortals,
who inhabit the city of
Pallas! Revering well
my sojourn among you, you shall never
blame the fortunes of life.

sp.speaker: Athena
sp.l: I praise the words of these prayers,
and I will escort you by the glow of bright-flaming torches
to the places below and beneath the earth,
together with the attendants who rightly guard
my image. For the eye of all the land
of Theseus shall come forth, a glorious band
of children, women, and a throng of elder women.
Honor them in crimson-dyed
robes, and let the glow of fire advance,
so that this kindly company of the land
may shine forth hereafter in fortunes of brave men.

sp.speaker: Propompoi
sp.l: Go to your home, great, honor-loving
childless children of Night, under kindly escort;
keep holy silence, people of the land!

sp.speaker: Propompoi
sp.l: Beneath the primeval caverns of earth,
both winning high reverence with honors and sacrifices—
keep holy silence, all the people!

sp.speaker: Propompoi
sp.l: Gracious and well-disposed to the land,
come hither, Dread Goddesses, with fire-devouring
torch, rejoicing along the way.
Raise now the cry of triumph after our song!

sp.speaker: Propompoi
sp.l: Peace abides forever between the dwellers
and the citizens of Pallas: Zeus the all-seeing
and Fate have thus come together.
Raise now the cry of triumph after our song!
